title: Jimmy Blanton's tuberculosis in California
summary: Hinton tells how Ben Webster asked him to look after Blanton, left sick in a California rest home when Duke's band moved on.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Look, I just wanted to remind you of one beautiful thing about you, and I think it should be a matter in your history, Foots. When you and I were with Cab Calloway's band (I can't remember the year), we were in California... What is what ballroom we played in California? The Casa Manana or something like that?
Yeah... We played the Cotton Club, you know.
No, this wasn't the Cotton Club. I'm thinking about in the Thirties and early Forties. And Duke Ellington's band had just left there, and the very fabulous Jimmy Blanton had gotten sick.
He was sick, and the band had to leave him in California. The year escapes me right now, but I'm sure somebody (?) will remember when it was. [THIS WOULD BE 1941]
And Ben Webster said to me, knowing how much I respected Jimmy for his fabulous playing...

...and for what he and Duke had done with 'Pitter Panther Patter' and all those beautiful things which had been called by one of our writers at the time 'bass duets,' which now are right up with some of the greatest things that ever happened.

But during this time (I'm listing this because it should be a part of your record), Ben Webster came to me, and said, "Bear..." That's what they called Jimmy Blanton. He said, "Bear is very sick, and we had to put him in a rest home." He had tuberculosis. He was a beautiful young man of 22 years old who didn't drink or smoke, but he was very frail, and being in Duke Ellington's band and making those one-night stands and getting soaking wet, playing as hard as he played and as fabulous as he played, and taking them bus rides 200 or 300 miles, he contracted a cold, and he couldn't get out of it, couldn't shake it, until he contracted tuberculosis. Not because he was a drinker or a carouser.

And Ben suggested that I...since we were coming out on the same engagement, and Duke's band was leaving, they were leaving town... He said, "Be sure and look out for Bear" -- Blanton. And in those days, remember, we had no penicillin; this is before penicillin. I don't even think the sulfur drugs were even too prevalent. But anyway, the only thing they were doing for tuberculosis in those days was just rest, bed rest -- which was not quite enough for what he had contracted.
